screens.title: Creating Basic XR User Interfaces (UI)
screens.subtitle: Design and implement readable, interactive World Space UI for immersive XR

narration.text: In this lesson we will learn how to build simple, usable user interfaces inside an XR scene. XR UI is not just 2D pasted onto a view — it lives in three dimensions, so you must think about depth, scale, and how users point or touch elements. You will understand why World Space canvases are the recommended render mode, how the XR Graphic Raycaster and XR UI components make standard buttons and sliders interactable, and how to wire those controls to Unity Events and a small C# manager. We'll also practice a hands-on workflow that creates a floating UI panel with TextMeshPro text and a Press Me button, and test it using an XR Ray Interactor. This matters because poorly configured UI breaks presence, causes fatigue, or becomes unreachable. By the end of the lesson you'll be able to add a World Space canvas, enable XR interactivity, and connect controls to game logic, so your VR or AR interfaces feel integrated and comfortable. Consider the final challenge: add a slider that updates status text — a small step that demonstrates the full interaction chain from input to script.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: World Space Canvas + XR Graphic Raycaster + XR UI components form the basic pipeline to make Unity UI work naturally in XR.

narration.text: By the end of these exercises you will understand the practical differences between Canvas render modes, be able to create and size a World Space canvas, and make UI elements respond to XR input. You will configure XR Graphic Raycaster and XR UI bridge components so buttons, sliders, and toggles receive ray hits. You will also wire Unity Events to a small UI manager script and test behavior with an XR Ray Interactor. Each objective is chosen because XR UI is different from flat 2D UI — you must consider scale, distance, and interaction modality. For example, a button that looks fine on screen space overlay may be unreadable or unreachable in VR. This screen presents four core objectives with short why-it-matters descriptions and simple visual mnemonics to help you remember the interaction chain from input to script. Practice these skills in the hands-on activity to build muscle memory and debug common setup mistakes like missing the XR Graphic Raycaster.

screens.title: Why XR UI differs from 2D UI
screens.subtitle: Depth, viewpoints, and input methods change how interfaces behave

narration.text: XR user interfaces must be designed with three-dimensional thinking. Unlike 2D screen interfaces, XR UI can be viewed from different angles and distances, so elements must remain legible and reachable across real head movements. Depth and parallax matter because they inform the user's sense of presence; UI that floats unrealistically or snaps to the camera can break immersion. Input methods also differ: rather than mouse and touch, XR uses rays, gaze, and direct hand interactions. This means a button must receive ray hits and should be large enough to tolerate small aiming errors. A concrete example is a floating control panel in front of the user: its scale should be set so text is readable from typical headset viewing distances, and the panel's surface must have an XR Graphic Raycaster so a ray pointer can trigger a button. A common misconception is treating Screen Space Overlay as acceptable in VR; it will appear fixed to the eyes and flatten depth, reducing realism. Key takeaway: design for physical space — size UI in meters, test readability inside an HMD, and prefer interactions that require comfortable pointing rather than precise finger movements. How will you check that your panel feels comfortable in VR?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: XR UI requires 3D placement, readable scale in meters, and interaction components that support spatial input methods.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Why XR UI differs
XR UI vs 2D UI
Three-dimensional context changes legibility, interaction, and perceived depth.
  • Depth & Perspective
    UI should respect world depth so users see consistent parallax and distance cues.
  • Input Modality
    Rays, gaze, and direct touch require different collider and component setups than mouse clicks.
  • Readability
    Fonts and control sizes must be tuned for viewing distance in meters, not pixels on a screen.
Key Takeaway

Design UI as physical objects: set scale in meters, add ray-aware components, and test inside the headset.

Analogy
Treat your UI like a physical control panel in the real world — place it at reachable height, make labels big enough to read from a comfortable distance, and avoid tiny targets.
Common mistake
Using Screen Space Overlay in XR because it’s quick. That flattens depth and detaches UI from the world, reducing presence.
Check your understanding
Can you read 12pt text at 1.5 meters in your headset? If not, increase font size or move the panel closer.

screens.title: Canvas Render Modes
screens.subtitle: Screen Space - Overlay, Screen Space - Camera, and World Space compared

narration.text: Unity provides three common canvas render modes, and choosing the right one determines whether your UI will feel like part of the environment. Screen Space Overlay draws UI on top of the frame and ignores world geometry — it's always visible but breaks immersion because it doesn't react to perspective. Screen Space Camera ties UI to a camera, which can be useful for mixed setups but still keeps UI flattened relative to the camera plane. World Space places the canvas as a 3D GameObject in the scene; it has a Rect Transform you can move, rotate, and scale so the UI becomes part of the environment. A practical example: a HUD that must always face the player might use Screen Space Camera, but a floating tablet on a desk must be World Space. Misconceptions arise when developers assume screen-space units translate directly to meters — they don't. For World Space, set pixel dimensions and then scale the canvas to match meters, e. g. a 1000x1000 canvas scaled to 0.001 becomes roughly one meter wide. Test each mode in context: for true immersion and correct depth, prefer World Space in XR.

keyIdea.title: Comparison summary
keyIdea.text: Overlay: always-on but flat; Camera: camera-relative flat plane; World Space: 3D object with depth — recommended for XR.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Canvas Render Modes
Screen Space - Overlay
Draws UI on top of everything, ignores depth. Fast for menus but unsuitable for immersive VR dashboards.
Screen Space - Camera
Renders to a specific camera; remains camera-relative and flattened, useful for mixed camera effects but still not truly 3D.
World Space
Acts as a 3D object. Set Render Mode to World Space and treat the canvas like a physical panel. Recommended for XR.
Practical hint
Use pixel size + small uniform scale for World Space. Example: 1000x1000 canvas scaled to 0.001 yields ~1 meter.
Visual rule-of-thumb
If you need UI to live on objects, be reachable, or obey perspective, choose World Space.
Check your understanding
  • - Would a floating tablet be best as Overlay, Camera, or World Space?
  • - Does pixel size alone determine world size? (Hint: use scale.)
Common mistake
Not scaling pixel-based canvases for world meters, resulting in panels that are too large or small in VR.

screens.title: Create a World Space Canvas — Step-by-step
screens.subtitle: From Hierarchy to visible 3D UI surface

narration.text: Follow a consistent process when creating a World Space canvas to avoid visibility and interaction problems. First, in the Hierarchy, create an empty GameObject for your panel and place it where the player can reach, for example at x=0, y=1.5, z=2. Next, add a new UI Canvas as a child of that GameObject. In the Inspector change Render Mode to World Space. Set the Rect Transform width and height to values like 500 by 300, then apply a uniform scale such as 0.002 to convert pixel dimensions into world meters. The scaling step is essential: without it, the canvas uses pixels and will appear mis-sized. After sizing, add visible UI children: a TextMeshPro text element and a Button. Import TMP essentials if prompted. Finally, add the XR Graphic Raycaster component to the World Space Canvas so XR rays can detect hits. Example: a 500x300 canvas scaled to 0.002 yields a 1x0.6 meter panel — test by placing it near the XR Origin and entering Play Mode. Misconception: neglecting the Graphic Raycaster is the most common reason buttons don’t respond to ray pointers.

keyIdea.title: Process
keyIdea.text: Create panel → add Canvas → set Render Mode to World Space → size and scale → add UI children → attach XR Graphic Raycaster.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Create a World Space Canvas
Steps
1. Create UIPanel GameObject
Place roughly at head height in front of the player, e.g., 0,1.5,2.
2. Add UI > Canvas
In Inspector, set Render Mode to World Space immediately.
3. Set Rect Transform
Width 500, Height 300, Scale 0.002 uniform to convert to meters.
4. Add TMP Text & Button
Import TMP essentials if needed and position elements within the canvas.
5. Add XR Graphic Raycaster
This allows XR Ray Interactors to target UI elements on the canvas.
Test
Enter Play Mode and verify ray pointer highlights the button and triggers On Click events.
Sizing example
500x300 canvas scaled to 0.002 gives approximately 1.0m by 0.6m. Adjust scale for comfortable reach and readability.
Common mistake
Leaving default scale or forgetting the XR Graphic Raycaster. If the button doesn’t respond, check for the missing raycaster first.
Why it matters
A correctly sized and ray-enabled canvas lets users interact comfortably and preserves immersion, reducing testing friction later.

screens.title: RectTransform, Pixels, and World Scale
screens.subtitle: Convert pixel sizes to meters and avoid sizing mistakes

narration.text: RectTransform controls a canvas's internal pixel dimensions while scale converts those pixels into world meters. Unity UI elements are laid out in pixels by default, so a 1000x1000 canvas is measured in pixels inside the component. To use that canvas as a physical panel, apply a uniform scale that maps pixels to meters. A common practical conversion is scaling 1000 pixels to 1 meter by setting the canvas scale to 0.001 on all axes. For example, a status panel that's 800 by 400 pixels and scaled to 0.001 will become 0.8 by 0.4 meters in world space. An important pitfall is non-uniform scaling — scaling X, Y, and Z differently will distort UI and make collider sizes inconsistent. Also be aware of the Canvas Scaler component; for World Space canvases you often disable automatic scaling or set it intentionally because automatic screen-size-based scaling is designed for screen-space UI. Concrete example: create a 500x300 canvas, set scale to 0.002, then position it at the player's eye height. Misconception: pixel values are not the same as meters — always test inside the HMD and iterate on scale until text and controls feel right.

keyIdea.title: Sizing rule
keyIdea.text: Use pixel dimensions for layout, then apply a uniform scale to convert to world meters; test in HMD and avoid non-uniform scaling.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › RectTransform & Scale
RectTransform → Pixels; Scale → Meters
Use pixel dimensions to place UI elements, then apply a uniform scale to set world size.
Sizing example
1000x1000 canvas scaled to 0.001 ≈ 1 x 1 meter. 500x300 with 0.002 ≈ 1 x 0.6 meters.
Common mistake
Non-uniform scaling distorts layout and hit detection. Always use the same value for X, Y, Z when scaling canvases.
Canvas Scaler note
The Canvas Scaler is helpful for screen-space UI. For World Space, disable or configure it intentionally to avoid unwanted pixel scaling behavior.
Check: hands-on
Create two canvases with different pixel sizes and the same scale. Compare their apparent world sizes to confirm the scale mapping.
Why it matters
Correct scaling avoids unreadable text and unreachable controls, and it ensures consistent interaction geometry for raycasts and direct touches.

screens.title: Standard UI Elements in World Space
screens.subtitle: Buttons, Text (TextMeshPro), Sliders and Toggles

narration.text: Standard Unity UI elements work in World Space the same way they do in screen space, but with a few setup differences. TextMeshPro provides crisp, readable text that is well-suited to XR — import TMP Essentials if Unity prompts you. Buttons, sliders, and toggles can be added as children of the World Space Canvas and laid out with RectTransforms. However, they will not receive XR interaction by default. To make them respond to ray pointers or direct touches, attach the XR UI equivalents provided by the XR Interaction Toolkit: XR UI Button, XR UI Slider, or XR UI Toggle. These components translate XR interaction into UnityEvent callbacks like On Click or On Value Changed so you can hook them to scripts. A concrete example: add a TextMeshPro text labeled 'Status' and a Button labeled 'Press Me'. Add XR UI Button to the Button and XR Graphic Raycaster to the canvas. If the Button still doesn't respond, confirm the ray interactor includes the canvas layer in its Interaction Layer Mask. Misconception: adding an XR Interactor alone is not sufficient — the canvas needs the Graphic Raycaster and the UI elements need XR UI bridge components.

keyIdea.title: UI elements note
keyIdea.text: Add TMP text and standard UI controls as children of a World Space canvas and attach XR UI bridge components to enable XR interaction.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Standard UI Elements
Common elements
Buttons, TextMeshPro text, sliders, and toggles are UI building blocks. In World Space they render as meshes on a plane.
TextMeshPro
Use TMP for sharp text. Assign a TextMeshProUGUI to your UIManager to update text at runtime.
XR UI bridge components
Add XR UI Button / Slider / Toggle to bridge standard UI events with XR Interaction Toolkit events.
Concrete example
Create StatusText (TMP) and ActionButton (Button). Add XR UI Button to ActionButton, then attach a Unity Event to call UIManager.OnButtonClicked.
Common mistake
Expecting native UI elements to respond to XR rays without adding XR UI components and the XR Graphic Raycaster.
Try this
Add a slider and confirm On Value Changed fires to update a text field — this validates both ray hits and event wiring.

screens.title: XR Graphic Raycaster — Making Canvas Ray-Aware
screens.subtitle: Enable ray detection so ray interactors can hit UI elements

narration.text: The XR Graphic Raycaster is the component that connects the XR Interaction Toolkit's ray system to Unity UI elements on a World Space canvas. Without it, raycast queries will ignore UI graphics and pass through the canvas as if it were transparent. Add the XR Graphic Raycaster to the World Space Canvas and ensure you have the appropriate interaction module set up on your ray interactor. Also check the canvas's layer: your XR Ray Interactor uses an Interaction Layer Mask to select targets, so your canvas must be on an included layer. A concrete example: add XR Graphic Raycaster to WorldSpaceUI, then set the XR Ray Interactor's Interaction Layer Mask to include the 'UI' layer you placed the canvas on. When the ray intersects a button, the Graphic Raycaster converts the hit into an event and the XR UI Button component triggers the UnityEvent. Common misconception: thinking Physics Raycast settings are enough. UI uses Graphic Raycaster specifically for Canvas graphics, so verify you added the correct component. The key takeaway is that the XR Graphic Raycaster is the glue that makes canvas graphics respond to XR rays.

keyIdea.title: Raycaster role
keyIdea.text: XR Graphic Raycaster processes ray hits on canvas graphics and enables XR UI bridge components to fire Unity Events.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › XR Graphic Raycaster
What it does
Processes ray hits on Canvas graphics and converts them into UI events that XR UI components can use.
Setup checklist
  • - Add XR Graphic Raycaster to the World Space Canvas.
  • - Place the canvas on a layer included in your XR Ray Interactor's Interaction Layer Mask.
  • - Ensure UI elements have XR UI bridge components (e.g., XR UI Button).
Debug tip
If nothing registers, check the Console for pointer logs and confirm the ray interactor is active and targeting the UI layer.
Concrete example
Add XR Graphic Raycaster to WorldSpaceUI. Set the ray interactor to include layer 'UI'. Point and verify the button highlights and triggers the event.
Common misconception
Relying only on physics raycasts for UI. Graphic Raycaster is required for Canvas graphics.

screens.title: Configure XR Ray Interactor for Distant Interaction
screens.subtitle: Layer masks and validating hits from afar

narration.text: Distant interaction uses an XR Ray Interactor to point at UI from a distance. To ensure it hits your World Space canvas, first confirm your ray interactor exists on your controllers or hands and is enabled. Next, set the Interaction Layer Mask on the XR Ray Interactor so it includes the layer your canvas and UI elements are on. This tells the interactor which objects to consider during raycasts. Then test the ray: when it intersects the canvas, the XR Graphic Raycaster will process the hit and let the XR UI Button trigger its UnityEvent. Concrete example: assign your canvas to a dedicated 'UI' layer, and set the ray interactor mask to include 'Default' and 'UI'. If the ray reaches the canvas but no event fires, check that the canvas has an XR Graphic Raycaster and the UI child has an XR UI Button. A common mistake is leaving the Interaction Layer Mask empty or omitting the canvas layer. Finally, tune ray length and hit behavior so the ray doesn't penetrate thin UI panels; use a visible reticle or pointer to give users aiming feedback. This ensures consistent distant interaction across scenes.

keyIdea.title: Interaction layer
keyIdea.text: Use the Interaction Layer Mask to include the canvas layer so XR Ray Interactors can target UI elements for distant interaction.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Configure XR Ray Interactor
Interaction Layer Mask
Assign canvas to a 'UI' layer and include that layer in the ray interactor mask to enable hits.
Checklist
  • - Canvas assigned to UI layer
  • - XR Graphic Raycaster present on canvas
  • - XR UI Button on button elements
  • - Ray Interactor mask includes UI layer
Tuning
Adjust ray length and pointer visuals to help aiming. Use a reticle on hit to confirm target selection.
Concrete example
Set canvas to 'UI' layer. In XR Ray Interactor, add 'UI' to Interaction Layer Mask. Point and confirm the button highlights and triggers the event.
Common mistake
Forgetting to set the canvas layer or leaving the interactor mask unset — resulting in invisible, untargetable UI.

screens.title: Direct Interaction vs Ray Interaction
screens.subtitle: When to use XR Direct Interactor and XR Grab Interactable

narration.text: Direct interaction means physically touching or grabbing objects with hand controllers or tracked hands, using XR Direct Interactor and XR Grab Interactable. Ray interaction uses a pointer from a distance, using XR Ray Interactor and XR UI bridge components. For UI, ray interaction is typically more comfortable and precise because it avoids sustained arm extension and is compatible with small targets. Direct interaction is useful when UI is part of a tangible object, like a tablet you pick up and hold. Concrete example: a floating tablet with a panel of buttons might be made grab interactable so the user can take it into their hands; inside that tablet the UI can still be a World Space Canvas with XR Graphic Raycaster so touch or finger events are possible. A common misconception is that direct interaction always feels more natural — in practice, it can cause fatigue and requires precise collision setup. Key takeaway: choose ray interaction for distant controls and direct/grab interaction for physical objects containing UI, and ensure colliders, interaction components, and event bridges match the chosen modality. Direct Interaction vs Ray Interaction means use ray interaction for distant ui; use direct/grab when ui is embedded in a physical object the user holds.. In practical terms, when to use xr direct interactor and xr grab interactable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Interaction choice
keyIdea.text: Use ray interaction for distant UI; use direct/grab when UI is embedded in a physical object the user holds.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Direct vs Ray Interaction
XR Ray Interactor
Best for distant UI. Uses a visible or invisible ray to point at UI elements and trigger events remotely.
XR Direct Interactor
Enables touch and grab mechanics for objects close to the hand, often used with XR Grab Interactable on physical items that contain UI.
Concrete scenario
A tablet: make it XR Grab Interactable so the user can pick it up. Inside, the tablet hosts a World Space canvas with XR Graphic Raycaster so buttons remain interactable while held.
Common mistake
Using direct interaction for all UI assuming it’s always more immersive — this often increases fatigue and complexity.

screens.title: UIManager Script — Wiring UI to Logic
screens.subtitle: Simple C# handlers for button clicks and slider changes

narration.text: A small manager script is all you need to react to UI events in XR. The UIManager holds references to a TextMeshProUGUI status field and exposes public methods for the button On Click and slider On Value Changed events. When the button fires, update the status text and log a message to the Console. When the slider value changes, format the value and display it. Concrete example: attach UIManager to a GameLogic object and drag the StatusText reference into the inspector. Then select the button's On Click event, add GameLogic, and choose UIManager. OnButtonClicked. A common pitfall is forgetting to assign the TextMeshPro reference, which results in null reference errors at runtime. Another mistake is wiring events on the wrong GameObject instance. Check your Inspector wiring and test in Play Mode. This code-focused lesson shows a concise, robust pattern for connecting UI to game logic in an XR scene. UIManager Script — Wiring UI to Logic means expose public methods on a manager object and connect them to unity events on xr ui elements to react to user actions.. In practical terms, simple c# handlers for button clicks and slider changes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Script pattern
keyIdea.text: Expose public methods on a manager object and connect them to Unity Events on XR UI elements to react to user actions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › UIManager Script
Script example
Attach this script to a GameLogic object and assign StatusText in the inspector. Wire button On Click to OnButtonClicked and slider On Value Changed to OnSliderValueChanged.
<!-- C# UIManager (escaped for HTML) -->
using UnityEngine;
using TMPro; // If using TextMeshPro

public class UIManager : MonoBehaviour
{
  [SerializeField] private TextMeshProUGUI statusText; // Assign in Inspector

  public void OnButtonClicked()
  {
    Debug.Log("UI Button Clicked!");
    if (statusText != null)
    {
      statusText.text = "Button Pressed!";
    }
  }

  public void OnSliderValueChanged(float value)
  {
    Debug.Log("Slider value: " + value);
    if (statusText != null)
    {
      statusText.text = $"Slider: {value:F2}";
    }
  }
}
Concrete wiring steps
Create GameLogic, attach UIManager, drag StatusText into the field. On Button > On Click, add GameLogic and select UIManager.OnButtonClicked.
Common mistake
Not assigning the TextMeshProUGUI reference results in no visible update. Always verify inspector references before Play Mode.
Key takeaway
Small, focused scripts plus Unity Events make UI logic easy to wire and test in XR.

screens.title: Build a Basic World Space Panel — Guided Lab
screens.subtitle: Follow these steps to create the sample UI and test interaction

narration.text: Let's walk through the lab workflow from the chapter. Start with a scene that contains an XR Origin and XR Ray Interactors on each controller. Create an empty GameObject named UIPanel and place it at 0, 1.5, 2. Right-click UIPanel and choose UI > Canvas; rename it WorldSpaceUI and set Render Mode to World Space. Set Rect Transform width to 500 and height to 300, then set Scale to 0.002 on all axes. Add XR Graphic Raycaster to the WorldSpaceUI. Add UI children: TextMeshPro - name it StatusText with initial text 'Welcome to XR!' and a Button - name it ActionButton with text 'Press Me'. Add XR UI Button to ActionButton. Create a GameLogic empty GameObject and attach the UIManager script. Drag StatusText into the UIManager's Status Text field. Select ActionButton's Button component, add a new On Click event, drag GameLogic into the slot, and select UIManager. OnButtonClicked. Enter Play Mode and point the ray at the button — it should highlight and fire the event, updating StatusText and logging to the Console. If it doesn't, check the Interaction Layer Mask and confirm XR Graphic Raycaster is present. This lab validates the full chain from canvas setup to runtime response.

keyIdea.title: Lab flow
keyIdea.text: Follow the sequence: setup XR Origin → create UIPanel → World Space canvas → add XR Graphic Raycaster → add UI elements → attach XR UI components → wire Unity Events → test.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Hands-on Activity
Activity: Build a World Space UI Panel
Step through the checklist and verify each stage in Play Mode.
Scene setup
Ensure XR Origin and XR Ray Interactors exist on controllers.
UIPanel & Canvas
Create UIPanel at 0,1.5,2. Add Canvas, set Render Mode to World Space.
Rect Transform
Width 500, Height 300, Scale 0.002 uniform.
XR Graphic Raycaster
Add this component to the canvas to enable ray hits.
UI Elements
Add TextMeshPro StatusText and Button ActionButton. Add XR UI Button to the Button.
Scripting & Wiring
Attach UIManager to GameLogic, assign StatusText, and link Button On Click to UIManager.OnButtonClicked.
Test checklist
Enter Play Mode, point with the ray, confirm the button highlights, press it, and check that StatusText updates and Console logs appear.
Troubleshooting
If the button doesn't respond, verify XR Graphic Raycaster, canvas layer, and the ray interactor's Interaction Layer Mask include that layer.
Extension challenge
Add a slider to the panel and wire On Value Changed to UIManager.OnSliderValueChanged so the status shows the slider value.

screens.title: Readability, Interaction Distance, and Comfort
screens.subtitle: Design choices that reduce fatigue and improve usability

narration.text: When designing XR UI, prioritize readability and comfort to avoid user fatigue. Readability depends on font size, contrast, and viewing distance: text should be large enough to be legible at the panel's typical distance. Interaction distance matters: UI placed too close forces head or arm strain, while UI placed too far reduces precision. Aim for reachable panels within comfortable arm range or rely on ray interaction for distant controls. Avoid interfaces requiring sustained, precise finger movements; those quickly tire users. A concrete guideline: test elements at intended placements in an HMD and iterate. High contrast between text and background improves perceptibility, and avoid overly dense information on a single panel. Misconception: piling many small controls onto a single panel because they fit visually; in XR, chunk controls into logical groups and prefer larger touch targets. Also test lighting and occlusion in AR contexts. Key takeaway: design for human comfort first — a usable UI is more important than fitting many features on one panel. Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Readability & Comfort
Design for comfort
A comfortable UI reduces fatigue and increases task success in XR.
Readability
Use larger fonts, strong contrast, and generous spacing. Test text at intended viewing distance inside the headset.
Interaction distance
Place common controls within comfortable reach or enable ray interaction. Avoid requiring extended arm holds.
Chunking & density
Group related controls and avoid cramming many small targets. Larger targets improve hit success for pointer-based input.
Testing tip
Always validate UI in an HMD using the exact scale and placement to catch readability and reachability issues early.
Key Takeaway
Human comfort drives good XR UI — prioritize readable text, reachable controls, and minimal sustained effort.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential concepts to carry forward. First, prefer World Space canvases in XR because they allow UI to exist in the scene and preserve depth and perspective. Second, add an XR Graphic Raycaster to World Space canvases so ray interactors can detect UI elements — without this, rays will pass through. Third, use XR UI bridge components such as XR UI Button, Slider, and Toggle to translate XR hits into Unity Events that you can wire to scripts. Fourth, convert pixel dimensions to world meters by applying a uniform scale to the canvas, and always test inside an HMD for readability and reachability. Finally, choose interaction modes carefully: use rays for distant interaction and direct/grab interactables for physical objects that users should pick up. Keep these concepts in mind as you build real XR panels and debug common issues like missing raycasters or wrong interaction layer masks. Which concept will you test first in your scene?

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders for building XR UI

narration.text: Keep these three compact reminders when you return to the editor. First, always test UI inside the headset at intended scale and distance to catch readability and reach issues early. Second, ensure your World Space canvas has an XR Graphic Raycaster and that the ray interactor's Interaction Layer Mask includes the canvas layer; missing this is the single most frequent setup error. Third, connect XR UI elements to Unity Events and small focused scripts like UIManager to keep logic simple and inspector-driven. These three checks — read/test, raycaster+layers, and event wiring — often resolve the majority of common XR UI problems. As you practice, build small test panels that exercise these checks before you add many controls to a scene.
